author: ValWood
body: This paper: Abstract We report the isolation of the mouse Kin17 gene, located on chromosome 2, coding a nuclear Zn-finger protein that has a 39-residue region homologous to Escherichia coli RecA protein and that is recognized by anti-RecA antibodies. Kin17 protein preferentially binds to curved DNA in vitro and in vivo, suggesting a role in illegitimate recombination and in regulation of gene expression. We have shown that the Kin17 gene is about 8 kb in length and displays three exons and two introns. The 5' flanking region lacks a canonical TATAA box but presents several putative regulatory domains. A major transcription initiation site is located 322 nucleotides upstream of the translation start site. The 1.7-kb transcript of the Kin17 gene is weakly and ubiquitously expressed in murine tissues and cell lines as determined by Northern analysis. The cross-hybridization of Kin17 cDNA with the genomic DNA of other species in Southern analysis indicates the conservation of the gene among mammals and suggests that the Kin17 gene plays a conserved role in DNA metabolism. doesn't provide evidence for a "DNA metabolism process" I'm looking at these to confirm the prediction for an unknown, and can't find any concrete evidence for any of these. If the DNA damage response" IEP annotation is removed, that will deal with the inferences. Let me know if you disagree. v

author: ValWood
body:
I can't access this paper [PMID:12359749], but  from the abstract I would flag this  "suggestion" 

Abstract
Kin17 is an evolutionarily conserved DNA-binding protein, which forms intranuclear foci in proliferating cells. Recent data have suggested that human kin17 protein is associated with cell proliferation and unrepaired DNA lesions. Herein, we show that human fibroblasts (MRC5-V2 and CHSV4) immortalized with SV40 overexpress endogenous kin17 protein, as compared with normal diploid human fibroblasts. We observed that certain carcinoma cell lines also up-regulated kin17 protein, suggesting that increased kin17 protein levels may be a consequence of the immortalized phenotype. We report here that the endogenous kin17 protein is located in nucleoplasmic foci and colocalizes with SV40 large T antigen. Purification of human kin17 protein allowed analysis of the physical interaction with T antigen by several in vitro and in vivo assays. Large T antigen and human kin17 protein are part of the same high molecular weight multiprotein complex in human cells. Furthermore, human kin17 protein interacts with T antigen bound to the SV40 DNA origin of replication. Strikingly, the overexpression of human kin17 protein in vivo and the introduction of increased amounts of human kin17 protein in an in vitro assay reduced T-antigen-dependent DNA replication, suggesting that kin17 protein may be involved in the DNA replication process in human cells.

@pgaudet  thoughts?

author: ValWood
body:
Claude summary:

Yes, these are orthologs. S. cerevisiae RTS2 is the yeast counterpart of mammalian KIN17 (gene symbol KIN). The yeast protein is much less well characterised.

S. cerevisiae Rts2 (YOR077W)
The NCBI/Alliance annotation says it is predicted to bind DNA and zinc, is found in the cytoplasm and nucleus, and is orthologous to human KIN (Kin17). 
[nih](https://https.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/854244)
BioGRID describes it as a basic zinc-finger protein, similar to the human and mouse Kin17 proteins, which are chromatin-associated and involved in the UV response and DNA replication. 
[thebiogrid](https://thebiogrid.org/34476)
It is small. Rts2 is 232 amino acids, and its Biological Process and Molecular Function GO terms are still "ND" (no data). Human KIN17 is 393 aa. So in practice the yeast gene has localisation data and a homology-based annotation, but no established function. Most of what is known comes from large-scale screens; BioGRID lists about 90 mostly high-throughput interactions. 
[yeastrc](https://www.yeastrc.org/pdr/viewProtein.do?id=533822)
Mammalian KIN17

The mammalian protein has more parts than Rts2: an N-terminal zinc finger, a winged-helix domain, and a C-terminal tandem SH3-like/KOW region. Its proposed roles fall into two groups:

DNA-related roles (the older literature). It was found through RecA cross-reactivity, it binds chromatin and DNA, it forms nuclear foci during proliferation, and it has been linked to the UV/DNA-damage response and to DNA replication. Much of this rests on localisation and correlation rather than clear mechanism.
Splicing (the newer and stronger evidence). KIN17 has been found in purified human spliceosomes and appears in cryo-EM structures of them. In a C. elegans genetic screen, KIN17 and PRCC were shown to be involved in splice site choice. Structural modelling places KIN17 near the U6/pre-mRNA helix in the human pre-Bact2 complex. Transcriptome-wide, though, the effects were modest: mutations in PRCC but not KIN17 changed 5′ splice sites genome-wide, while mutations in both changed dozens of 3′ splice sites. 
PLoS Genetics (Feb 2022)
 +2
Points to keep in mind when comparing them
Domains. Rts2 is about 60% the length of KIN17. Before transferring any function, align the two (with InterPro or an AlphaFold superposition) to see which mammalian domains Rts2 actually has. My expectation, which I haven't confirmed, is that the N-terminal zinc finger and winged helix are conserved and the C-terminal KOW region is not.
Splicing context. Budding yeast has few introns and a simplified spliceosome, and as far as I know Rts2 isn't a recognised component of the yeast spliceosome structures. So the splicing role seen in metazoans may not carry over to S. cerevisiae. S. pombe, which has many introns, would be a better comparison point.
Strength of evidence. The mammalian DNA-repair/replication role is the part most often cited in yeast annotations. It is also arguably the least mechanistically established.

I can run the Rts2 vs human/mouse KIN17 domain alignment for you, or pull the high-throughput hits for Rts2 (genetic and physical interactions, deletion phenotypes) to see whether any point toward DNA damage or RNA processing.
